text:
Ask NLTK's lemmatizer for the dictionary form of running, and you get running back. Ran stays ran. And was comes back as wa. It isn't broken. Unless you say otherwise, it treats every word as a noun. It sees one word at a time, never the sentence, so it can't tell what job that word is doing. And running really can be a noun, as in the running of the race. As a noun, it's already a dictionary form. So what does the lookup actually do?

It takes three steps. First, each part of speech keeps a list of irregular forms. As a verb, ran is listed under run, and was under be. As an adjective, better is listed under good and well. If a word isn't listed, suffix rules make the guesses instead, like a noun's s, or a verb's ed or ing. Last, the word and every guess are checked against WordNet. Only real entries survive, and the shortest one wins. That's where wa comes from. Was isn't on the noun list, so the s comes off, and wa is a real entry: it's short for Washington, the state. Running passes as itself. But ran isn't a noun at all, so nothing survives, and you just get ran back. So where does the part of speech come from?

From a tagger, which reads the whole sentence. Take the runners were running and they had eaten well. It gives each word a Penn Treebank tag: NNS for runners, VBD for were, VBG for running. WordNet knows just four parts of speech, so keep each tag's first letter. J is an adjective, V a verb, R an adverb, and anything else, a noun. Now lemmatize with those. Runners becomes runner, were becomes be, running run, had have, and eaten eat. Porter's stemmer gets runner and run, too. But were, had and eaten pass straight through, because it only cuts endings. So the lemmatizer was never broken. It needed the part of speech. Tag first, then lemmatize.
